Microstructure refers to the internal structure of geopolymer composites, including mullite crystal distribution and interlocking, which influences mechanical performance.<SEP>Microstructure refers to the internal structure of the composites analyzed in relation to their mechanical and physical properties, though specific details are not described in the text.<SEP>Microstructure refers to the internal structure of the geopolymer, analyzed using SEM and influenced by NaOH concentration as shown in Figure 7.

Fly Ash
Fly Ash (FA) is a by-product generated from coal combustion in electric power plants, primarily composed of 40–50 wt% silica (silicon dioxide), along with significant amounts of alumina (aluminum oxide), iron oxide, calcium oxide, magnesium oxide, sulfur oxide, potassium oxide, sodium, titanium dioxide, strontium oxide, phosphorus pentoxide, and residual carbon. It is characterized by spherical particles, including hollow cenospheres, with a particle size distribution ranging from less than 1 μm to over 50 μm, though the typical size is less than 20 μm, with approximately 10% of particles exceeding 30 μm. Its chemical composition and physical morphology make it suitable for various industrial applications.

Fly ash serves as a primary aluminosilicate source in the production of geopolymers. Due to its glassy structure, it can be dissolved under alkaline conditions when mixed with alkaline activators, enabling geopolymerization. In this context, it acts as a raw material in geopolymer mixtures, where its particle size distribution and chemical profile are critical for performance. It is widely used as a pozzolan in geopolymer synthesis and is valued for its reactivity in alkaline environments.

In addition to its role in geopolymer composites, fly ash is also utilized as a filler material in natural rubber (NR) composites. However, when used in rubber applications, it exhibits poorer dispersion within the matrix, leading to larger agglomerates and increased void content compared to geopolymer-based fillers. This results in weaker interfacial interactions with the rubber matrix and reduced thermal stability. Despite these limitations, fly ash is explored as a low-cost, natural filler alternative in rubber compounds, with ongoing research focusing on its characterization in terms of particle size, chemical composition, morphology, and effects on curing behavior.

In summary, fly ash is a versatile industrial byproduct with dual applications: as a key raw material in geopolymer production due to its reactive aluminosilicate content, and as a filler in natural rubber composites, where its performance is limited by dispersion challenges and inferior matrix compatibility compared to geopolymer fillers.

Laser Diffraction Analysis
Laser diffraction analysis is the method used to measure particle size distribution of fly ash and mullite powder, performed using a Malvern Instrument Mastersizer 2000.

Compressive Strength
Compressive strength is a mechanical property of geopolymer composites, measured in megapascals (MPa), that indicates the material's resistance to failure under compressive load. It was evaluated after 7 days of curing using a Universal Testing Machine, with each reported value representing the average of five samples. The addition of mullite, up to 40 wt%, significantly enhances compressive strength, as demonstrated by an increase from 14 MPa to 71 MPa in the geopolymer composite. This improvement is attributed not only to mullite incorporation but also potentially to reduced water content, although specific values related to the latter factor are not provided in the data. Overall, compressive strength is a key performance indicator influenced by both compositional and processing factors in geopolymer systems.

Optimum NaOH Concentration
The optimum NaOH concentration was determined to be 12 mol/l based on consistent compressive strength results and microstructural analysis.

Geopolymer
Geopolymer (GP) is an aluminosilicate-based inorganic polymer synthesized through the geopolymerization of fly ash and an alkaline activator, forming an amorphous three-dimensional network. It is primarily derived from fly ash, exhibiting a particle size range from less than 1 μm to over 50 μm, with a typical size under 20 μm, and features smooth surfaces and irregular shapes similar to its precursor material. Chemical composition analysis reveals that geopolymer contains higher levels of silicon dioxide and lower calcium oxide compared to raw fly ash, while FTIR spectroscopy confirms the presence of Si-O-T bond vibrations, indicating successful geopolymerization. 

In the context of rubber composites, geopolymer is used as a novel filler material in natural rubber (NR) vulcanizates. It demonstrates improved dispersion within the rubber matrix, particularly at an optimal loading of 10 parts per hundred rubber (phr), leading to more homogeneous distribution. Its incorporation influences cure characteristics, including torque development, cross-linking density, and cure rate, while also contributing to slightly enhanced thermal stability compared to unfilled NR. Additionally, geopolymer-filled composites exhibit improved mechanical and dynamic properties, making it a promising sustainable filler option. 

Beyond rubber applications, geopolymer is recognized as a composite material capable of achieving high compressive strength and reduced cracking under optimal conditions. In some studies, it has been modified with additives such as mullite to tailor physical properties like setting time. Overall, geopolymer serves as a versatile material—both as a high-performance construction binder and as a functional filler in natural rubber composites—leveraging waste-derived aluminosilicate sources for advanced material applications.

Mullite
Mullite is a ceramic material added to geopolymer composites to enhance compressive strength and modify microstructure, with optimal performance at 40 wt%.<SEP>Mullite is a ceramic material added to geopolymer mixtures, affecting setting time and water content. Its addition reduces initial setting time and proportionally decreases water content in the mixture.

Cylindrical PVC molds of dimensions ∅15 mm × 30 mm were used to cast the geopolymer samples during preparation.

The curing procedure involved heating samples at 90°C for 1 day followed by 40°C for 6 days to solidify the geopolymer-mullite composite.

Griffith's principle is cited to explain that specimens with larger pre-existing cracks exhibit lower compressive strength.

Natural Rubber Composites with Geopolymer Filler
The study titled 'Novel natural rubber composites with geopolymer filler' is a research activity investigating the properties of natural rubber composites using geopolymer particles as fillers.

Dynamic Properties
Dynamic properties of the NR/geopolymer composites were studied, with the Payne effect observed in the filled composites.<SEP>Dynamic properties refer to the viscoelastic behavior of rubber composites under cyclic loading, investigated in geopolymer or fly ash-filled NR composites.

Mechanical Properties
Mechanical properties include 100% modulus and tensile strength, which improved with the addition of 10 phr geopolymer in natural rubber composites.<SEP>Mechanical properties include tensile strength, Young's modulus, and elongation at break, which are evaluated in geopolymer or fly ash-filled natural rubber composites.<SEP>Mechanical properties of rubber composites are improved by geopolymer filler due to better dispersion and stronger filler-rubber interactions, as shown in Figure 9.

Hassarutai Yangthong
Hassarutai Yangthong is one of the researchers involved in the study on natural rubber composites with geopolymer filler.

Metal Oxide Impurities
Metal oxide impurities are present in geopolymer particles and are responsible for accelerating the curing process in natural rubber composites.

Cure Characteristics
Cure characteristics describe the vulcanization behavior of rubber composites, which are influenced by the addition of fillers like geopolymers, fly ash, and RHA.<SEP>Cure characteristics refer to the changes in curing behavior of natural rubber composites when geopolymer particles are added, including faster curing due to metal oxide impurities.

Morphological Properties
Morphological properties of the NR/geopolymer composites were investigated as part of the study.<SEP>Morphological properties refer to the microstructure and filler dispersion in rubber composites, analyzed in geopolymer or fly ash-filled NR composites.

Thermal Properties
Thermal properties describe how rubber composites respond to heat, including stability and degradation, and were studied in geopolymer or fly ash-filled NR composites.<SEP>Thermal properties were enhanced in the geopolymer-filled natural rubber composites, showing improved thermal stability.

Natural Rubber
Natural Rubber (NR), also known as polyisoprene, is a base polymer and serves as the polymer matrix in various composite materials, particularly in studies involving the incorporation of fillers such as geopolymer and fly ash. It is used in the preparation of NR/geopolymer composites and functions as the primary material for evaluating the effects of these fillers on curing behavior and material performance in vulcanizates. The natural rubber used in these studies is processed in the form of air-dried sheets sourced from Nabon Rubber Co., Ltd. As a key component in composite systems, NR acts as the foundational material for experimental investigations into filler reinforcement and thermal stability. It undergoes thermal degradation between 330°C and 450°C, which is a critical factor in assessing its durability and application limits. Overall, Natural Rubber is central to the development and analysis of advanced composite materials, particularly in the context of geopolymer and fly ash integration.

GP Particles
GP particles are geopolymer particles used as fillers in natural rubber composites at various loadings (0, 10, 20, 30, 40 phr).

Renewable Resources
Renewable resources are alternative sources for fillers in rubber composites, of interest for improving sustainability and green aspects.

Carbon Black
Carbon black is a conventional synthetic filler used in rubber compounding for reinforcement and property enhancement.

Physical Interactions
Physical interactions between geopolymer particles and natural rubber molecules contribute to improved mechanical properties.

Payne Effect
The Payne effect describes the nonlinear decrease in storage modulus under increasing strain in filled rubber, related to filler-filler interactions, which was observed in the study of NR composites.<SEP>The Payne effect is observed in geopolymer-filled natural rubber composites, indicating nonlinear viscoelastic behavior typical of filled rubber systems.

Silica
Silica is a conventional synthetic filler used in rubber, known for reinforcing properties and hydrophilic surface characteristics.<SEP>Silica is mentioned as an important factor controlling geopolymerization and the structure of the final geopolymer.

Bagasse Fiber Ash
Bagasse fiber ash is a natural filler investigated for use in rubber composites.

Filler Loading
Filler loading refers to the amount of filler (e.g., GP or FA) added to the rubber matrix in phr (parts per hundred rubber); high GP content (30–40 phr) led to agglomeration and void formation.<SEP>Filler loading refers to the amount of filler (e.g., geopolymer or fly ash) added to natural rubber, expressed in parts per hundred rubber (phr), with optimal performance between 10–20 phr.<SEP>Filler loading refers to the amount of geopolymer added to natural rubber, specified in parts per hundred rubber (phr), tested at 0, 10, 20, 30, and 40 phr.

Industrial Applications
Industrial applications are potential uses for natural rubber composites with 10 phr geopolymer, suggested as suitable based on performance.

Synthetic Fillers
Synthetic fillers such as carbon black and silica are conventional reinforcing agents in rubber, contrasted with geopolymer in this study.
